Article Title: A Washington couple said their neighbour blocked a shared driveway, cut power to security cameras and turned off their water; an October 27 appeals court upheld the anti-harassment order protecting th
Article Text:
What the couple alleged

Why the court upheld the order

Why neighbour disputes can escalate

What protection orders can do

The wider lesson for homeowners

A long-running dispute between neighbours in Washington State has ended, at least for now, with a state appeals court backing an anti-harassment order that protects a couple who said their neighbour blocked a shared driveway, cut electricity to their security cameras and shut off their water. The Washington Court of Appeals, Division III, upheld the protection order on October 27, according to the published decision in case number 41231-8, via Justia Law.The case is a reminder that neighbour conflicts do not always remain minor disagreements over property lines, parking or maintenance. When a pattern of conduct begins to interfere with a family’s safety, access to their home or basic utilities, the law can treat it as harassment rather than an ordinary civil quarrel. In this dispute, the appellate court concluded that the lower court had sufficient grounds to keep the protective order in place.According to the account described in the appeals court record, the couple said the trouble began with the shared driveway outside their homes. They alleged that their neighbour blocked the driveway, making it harder for them to come and go from their property. For many households, a driveway is not simply a convenience.It can be the main route for emergency vehicles, deliveries, visitors and daily travel, so blocking it can quickly turn a property disagreement into a safety concern.The couple also said the neighbour interfered with the electricity supply to their security cameras. Security cameras are often installed to give homeowners peace of mind, especially when tensions with someone nearby are already high. If the power to those cameras is disrupted, residents may feel exposed and unable to document what is happening around their home. The court record indicates that the couple raised this alleged interference as part of their harassment claims.Perhaps most seriously, the couple alleged that their water was turned off. Access to running water is a basic household need, affecting drinking, cooking, sanitation and hygiene. An allegation that someone deliberately cut off another household’s water supply goes well beyond the kind of irritation that commonly arises between neighbours. It suggests conduct that can make a home difficult or unsafe to live in.The appeals court was asked to decide whether the anti-harassment order should remain in effect. After reviewing the case, the Division III court upheld the order on October 27. The decision means the protections granted to the couple will stand, subject to the terms set by the court.Washington’s anti-harassment laws allow courts to issue protection orders when someone engages in a course of conduct directed at another person that seriously alarms, annoys, harasses or harms them, and that serves no legitimate or lawful purpose. The conduct must also be serious enough that a reasonable person would suffer substantial emotional distress, and the person seeking protection must actually experience that distress.That legal standard matters because courts do not issue these orders over every unpleasant interaction. A single argument, a misplaced rubbish bin or a disagreement about who should repair a fence will not usually meet the threshold. But when actions accumulate into a pattern that interferes with someone’s ability to live safely and peacefully in their own home, a court may find that the behaviour crosses into unlawful harassment.In this case, the alleged conduct involved access to the property, surveillance equipment and an essential utility. Taken together, those allegations painted a picture of sustained interference rather than an isolated dispute. The appeals court’s decision to uphold the order suggests it found the trial court’s assessment of the evidence and the need for protection to be sound.Neighbour disputes often start over something small. A shared driveway can create confusion about who may park where, who is responsible for snow removal or repairs, and whether one household is blocking another’s access. Because both parties live side by side, there is no easy way to avoid contact, and small grievances can build over months or years.Disputes involving shared driveways, easements, fences, drainage, trees and boundaries are especially common because property records do not always answer every practical question. A driveway may be legally shared even if one neighbour has historically used it more often. A utility line may cross one property to serve another. Without clear communication, each side may believe the other is acting unreasonably.The danger is that frustration can lead to retaliation. Instead of resolving the underlying issue, one party may begin taking actions intended to pressure, punish or inconvenience the other. Blocking access, interfering with utilities or disabling security measures can feel like an escalation from disagreement to intimidation. Courts are particularly concerned when that conduct appears deliberate and continuing.An anti-harassment order can impose several kinds of restrictions. Depending on the facts, a court may prohibit contact, prevent a person from coming near the protected household, restrict surveillance, or order someone to stop specific conduct. The goal is not to punish the respondent through the order itself, but to prevent further harassment while the underlying issues are addressed through the proper legal channels.In earlier Washington cases, courts have upheld anti-harassment orders that barred neighbours from surveilling one another. In one Division Two case, the court affirmed an order preventing a neighbour from surveilling the people who sought protection, finding that Washington law expressly allows courts to prohibit attempts to keep a victim under surveillance.That does not mean every camera or every observation of a neighbour is illegal. People may have legitimate reasons to record activity on their own property, particularly if they are concerned about damage or safety. But when recording, monitoring or other conduct becomes part of a campaign aimed at frightening or controlling a neighbour, courts can consider it within the scope of harassment.For homeowners, the case highlights the importance of documenting problems early and seeking help before a conflict becomes dangerous. If a neighbour is blocking access to a shared driveway, repeatedly interfering with utilities or damaging security equipment, residents should keep dated records, photographs, messages and any other evidence that shows what happened and when.It is also wise to contact local authorities or a lawyer when essential services or safe access to a home are affected. A blocked driveway may require different help than a cut water line or a disabled security system, but all three can support a broader claim that a neighbour’s conduct has become more than a property disagreement.The October 27 ruling does not erase the underlying tension between the neighbours, and it does not decide every possible property-rights question that may exist between them. What it does do is confirm that the couple’s request for protection was legally justified. For them, the court’s decision provides a formal boundary and a measure of security after conduct they said made their home harder to live in.For everyone else, it offers a simple lesson: neighbours may disagree, but they cannot use access, utilities or fear as weapons. When a dispute becomes a pattern of interference, Washington courts have shown they are willing to step in.
Article Summary: Couple said their neighbour blocked a shared driveway, cut electricity to their security cameras and shut off their water. Washington Court of Appeals, Division III, upheld the protection order on October 27. Case is a reminder that neighbour conflicts do not always remain minor disagreements over property lines, parking or maintenance.

Article Title: An animal-borne virus called Shamonda, which normally circulates in livestock, has infected and killed a human for the first time on record, raising fresh questions about diseases that jump from anima
Article Text: For the first time, a human has contracted and died from the Shamonda virus, a disease-causing microbe that had previously been known only to infect animals. While the incident is unlikely to herald a more widespread outbreak, it is a potent reminder of the potential for pathogens to jump from animals to humans, with deadly consequences.As per a report by Scientific American, a 61-year-old man who was undergoing treatment for leukaemia at the Civil Hospital of Lyon in France contracted the disease. According to a case report published in Eurosurveillance, the man had undergone a stem cell transplant and experienced fatal encephalitis, or brain swelling. He showed symptoms, such as blindness and confusion, that the report authors say were likely caused by the virus. The man fell into a coma and succumbed to the disease on October 9, 2026, after life support was withdrawn. He is the first person ever known to have contracted the disease and died as a result.In a joint statement, the French Ministry of Health and Ministry of Agriculture said that they suspect the patient contracted the disease from a midge bite in eastern France, where the disease has been found in several animals. Officials have reported their findings to the World Health Organisation and the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC).The Shamonda virus was first identified in cattle in Nigeria in 1965. Spread by bites from tiny insects called Culicoides midges, it causes several symptoms in the animals, including fever, diarrhoea and reduced milk production. The virus has also been known to infect sheep, goats, horses and alpacas. Previously, cases have been detected in some African countries, Japan and—for the first time this summer—Europe. There are no vaccines to protect animals or people from Shamonda infections.Shamonda has been found in livestock in 14 European countries. Two new clades of the virus, SHAV-EU1 and SHAV-EU2, were detected earlier this year, and genetic testing revealed traces of the first type in the deceased person’s cerebrospinal fluid, urine and saliva, among other samples.The Shamonda virus is part of the Simbu serogroup and belongs to the genus Orthobunyavirus—the same serogroup and genus as the Oropouche virus, or sloth fever, which caused 9.4 million human infections in Latin America and the Caribbean regions from 1960 to 2025.As of now, experts have emphasised the need for caution. “At this stage, there is no evidence that the Shamonda virus will become more common in humans,” said clinical virologist Grégory Destras. He is affiliated with the same hospital in Lyon and is a co-author of the report. Destras notes that the virus may have spent several weeks incubating and multiplying in the patient before the neurological symptoms appeared.Natasha Tilston-Lunel, virologist at Indiana University School of Medicine, highlighted the Oropouche cases, but noted that the Schmallenberg virus, which is closely related to Shamonda has been found to be widespread in livestock but no humans. According to her, Shamonda may also have limited infectiousness among people. Continued surveillance of livestock and their aborted fetuses, insects and genomic sequencing of human samples, however, will be critical to detecting any changes to Shamonda’s risk in people, she said.Veterinary virologist Martin Beer of the Friedrich Loeffler Institute in Germany is part of a team that has conducted several studies of the Shamonda virus, including a recent preprint on the first evidence of its presence in European sheep and goats. Beer said that the main transmission route of viruses of the Simbu serogroup is biting midges, which can rapidly spread infections, especially in the summer and autumn. “In winter the transmission cycle stops since the number of biting midges is very low and temperatures below approximately 12 degrees Celsius do not allow efficient virus replication,” he said.A spokesperson for the ECDC told Scientific American that the agency needs clarity regarding the transmission of the virus and the role of vectors in infecting people. Destras suggested that retrospective analyses of stored samples from immunocompromised people could identify asymptomatic infections and the true scale of Shamonda in France.More studies to analyse antibody prevalence against Shamonda in people could give a clearer picture of whether this particular virus made the leap to humans before and they just didn’t realise it because no one died.
Article Summary: A 61-year-old man in France contracted and died from the Shamonda virus. He had undergone a stem cell transplant and experienced fatal encephalitis, or brain swelling. The man fell into a coma and succumbed to the disease on October 9, 2026, after life support was withdrawn. He is the first person ever known to have contracted the disease and died as a result.

Article Title: In 2002, a North Carolina city acquired flood-prone land; 24 years later, it has restored 27 acres of wetlands and streams, adding flood storage intended to protect up to 93 properties valued at about
Article Text:
North Carolina city restores 27 acres of wetlands to reduce flood risks for 93 properties (Image Credit: City of Hendersonville)

Why Hendersonville acquired the land in 2002

How the 27-acre restoration project works

Up to 93 properties could benefit from additional flood storage

Funding and partnerships helped bring the project to completion

A North Carolina city has completed the first phase of a floodplain restoration project more than two decades after acquiring land vulnerable to flooding. The City of Hendersonville’s Lower Mud Creek Floodplain Restoration Project has transformed approximately 27 acres into restored wetlands, streams, natural floodplain habitat and public green space. According to the city’s October 27, 2026, announcement, the project is expected to provide additional floodwater storage and reduce risks for as many as 93 nearby properties with an assessed value of approximately $60 million. A ribbon-cutting ceremony is scheduled for October 30 to mark the completion of Phase 1.The project centres on two city-owned properties along Mud Creek in the southside of Hendersonville, North Carolina. The city acquired the land in 2002 partly to preserve floodwater storage and prevent further development in an area vulnerable to flooding. Mud Creek has a long history of flooding. During the 19th and early 20th centuries, sections of the creek were straightened, dredged and separated from surrounding land by raised embankments, known as berms. These interventions were intended to drain the valley and make more land available for agriculture and development.Over time, commercial construction, filling of floodplain areas and changes to the stream system reduced the landscape’s natural ability to hold floodwater. The creek also became disconnected from parts of its floodplain, limiting the space available for water to spread during heavy rainfall. The restoration project seeks to reverse some of these changes by reconnecting the creek and its tributaries to the surrounding floodplain, allowing the landscape to perform its natural flood-management function.The project includes approximately 2,300 linear feet of tributary stream restoration and 1,500 linear feet of channel restoration along Mud Creek. It also involves restoring 8.5 acres of wetlands and restoring or enhancing approximately 9.2 acres of riparian floodplain, the areas alongside streams and waterways. These measures are designed to create more room for water during storms. The restored wetlands can collect and gradually release stormwater during smaller rainfall events, while the broader floodplain provides additional space for water to spread during larger floods.The project also incorporates water-control structures and native vegetation to support the restored landscape. Pedestrian bridges, approximately 2,500 linear feet of paved greenway and 1,600 linear feet of natural-surface trail are intended to make the site accessible to the public. The combination of flood management, habitat restoration and recreational infrastructure means the site is intended to serve several purposes rather than functioning solely as a drainage project.According to the city, the restored floodplain is expected to provide approximately 20 acre-feet of additional flood storage. One acre-foot represents enough water to cover one acre of land to a depth of one foot. The additional capacity is intended to help reduce flood risk for as many as 93 nearby properties, representing approximately $60 million in assessed value. The figure describes the assessed value of the properties potentially benefiting from reduced risk, rather than a guaranteed amount of financial savings or damage avoided.By giving floodwater more room to spread naturally, the project aims to reduce the pressure on nearby developed areas during heavy rainfall. The restoration is also expected to improve water quality by helping wetlands and vegetation filter runoff, while creating better habitat for aquatic life and other wildlife. However, the city’s announcement describes expected benefits. The additional storage does not mean flooding will be eliminated, particularly during severe weather events.The restoration took years of watershed planning, environmental assessments, engineering, grant development and coordination among public agencies and technical partners. In spring 2023, Hendersonville received grant funding through the North Carolina Land and Water Fund and the North Carolina Division of Water Infrastructure to support the design and construction of Phase 1. The wider project has also received support from the North Carolina Water Resources Development Grant Program, the North Carolina Flood Resiliency Blueprint and the city.Wildlands Engineering served as the project engineer, while Shamrock Environmental was responsible for construction. Land of Sky Regional Council, EcoForesters and other technical and regulatory partners also contributed to the initiative. The city announced that the first phase would be formally marked with a ribbon-cutting ceremony on October 30, 2026, at 519 South Grove Street in Hendersonville.The Lower Mud Creek project illustrates how land acquired for flood protection can eventually support a broader environmental and community benefit. By restoring wetlands and reconnecting streams to their floodplain, Hendersonville is seeking to improve its resilience to flooding while creating natural habitat and accessible green space for residents.
Article Summary: North Carolina city restores 27 acres of wetlands to reduce flood risks for 93 properties. A ribbon-cutting ceremony is scheduled for October 30 to mark the completion of Phase 1. The project centres on two city-owned properties along Mud Creek in the southside of Hendersonville, North Carolina.

Article Title: For more than 15 years, eight descendants negotiated the fate of inherited land along the Maryland-Delaware border; a conservation deal has now permanently protected 181 acres of forest and wetlands a
Article Text:
A family inheritance becomes a conservation priority

How the 181 acres will be protected

A wider impact on the Chesapeake Bay watershed

A conservation effort spanning more than 15 years has secured 181 acres of forests, wetlands and waterways along the Nanticoke River and Wright Creek, preserving ecologically significant land across Maryland and Delaware. The project, announced by the Nanticoke River Watershed Conservancy and Chesapeake Conservancy, brings together multiple generations of the Porter family, state conservation agencies and federal partners to protect the landscape from future development. The newly established Henry F. Porter Preserve in Delaware and the adjacent Porter Tract in Maryland form part of a wider effort to safeguard the Chesapeake Bay watershed, where forests, tidal creeks and wetlands support wildlife and help maintain the health of connected waterways.The project began more than 15 years ago, when the Nanticoke River Watershed Conservancy started working with eight descendants of Henry F. Porter to secure the future of their inherited property. Deeds and successive inheritances dating back to the mid-19th century complicated negotiations, requiring years of coordination among family members and conservation organisations.Porter purchased the land in 1950. To honour his legacy, the protected areas have been named after him, with the Delaware property becoming the Henry F.Porter Preserve and the Maryland parcel joining the state’s Chesapeake Forest Lands system.Chesapeake Conservancy subsequently helped advance the acquisition, purchasing the land temporarily while arrangements were made to transfer it into long-term conservation ownership. The initial acquisition comprised approximately 138 acres in Delaware and 39 acres in Maryland. The family later worked with the conservation organisations to protect an additional four wooded acres along Wright Creek.The conservation arrangement divides the land between the two states, with different agencies overseeing its long-term protection. In Maryland, the 39-acre tract was acquired by the Maryland Department of Natural Resources using Program Open Space funding. It has been incorporated into Chesapeake Forest Lands, a network spanning more than 75,000 acres across six Maryland counties. The property will be managed as a sustainable forest and is leased to a private hunting club.In Delaware, the 142-acre preserve has been transferred to the Nanticoke River Watershed Conservancy. A conservation easement held jointly by the US Navy and the Delaware Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control restricts future development to protect the land’s conservation value.Funding for the Delaware easement came through the state’s Open Space Program and the Department of Defense’s Readiness and Environmental Protection Integration (REPI) programme. REPI supports partnerships that protect land around military installations and testing areas, helping prevent incompatible development while preserving environmental resources. The preserve borders other protected areas, including the Nanticoke Wildlife Area and Pete Gum Preserve near Seaford, Delaware. Plans also include improving existing logging trails to make the property more accessible for hiking and nature study.Beyond protecting the property itself, the agreement strengthens a network of conserved landscapes in a region facing increasing development pressure. The Nanticoke watershed extends across roughly 725,000 acres and contains extensive tidal wetlands, forests and habitats for migratory birds and other wildlife.Local reporting by WBOC highlighted the project’s importance for water quality, particularly because forests and wetlands help limit sediment entering waterways. That matters for the wider Chesapeake Bay ecosystem, where changes in land use can affect aquatic habitats and the species that depend on them. The Nanticoke also supports important fish populations, including Atlantic sturgeon in its connected waterways.The project is also significant for its cross-border approach. Conservation officials have identified the need to protect connected habitats rather than isolated parcels, allowing wildlife to move through larger stretches of natural land while helping maintain ecological resilience. Chesapeake Conservancy has helped protect 26 properties covering 3,466 acres in the Nanticoke watershed with support from Mt. Cuba Center. The organisation has also identified more than 1,000 additional acres in the Mid-Atlantic Flyway that could offer substantial conservation benefits if protected.The Henry F. Porter Preserve represents a long-term investment in that broader effort, combining family stewardship, public funding and conservation partnerships to keep a landscape of forests and wetlands intact for future generations.As officials consider further opportunities to connect protected areas, the project offers an example of how sustained negotiations and cooperation between neighbouring states can deliver lasting environmental benefits.
Article Summary: conservation effort has secured 181 acres of forests, wetlands and waterways along the Nanticoke River and Wright Creek. Project brings together multiple generations of the Porter family, state conservation agencies and federal partners to protect the landscape from future development. The newly established Henry F. Porter Preserve in Delaware and the adjacent Porter Tract in Maryland form part of a wider effort to safeguard the Chesapeake Bay watershed.

Article Title: A 10-year-old Georgia boy wanted to help people experiencing homelessness; he spent two weeks selling bracelets and raised $400 to buy food and essential supplies
Article Text:
Images: WALB News

How a 10-year-old US boy raised $400 by selling bracelets

What he donated to the homelessness support organisation

What Graham's parents said about the initiative

How LAMP supports people experiencing homelessness

Graham hopes to continue helping others

A 10-year-old boy from Valdosta, Georgia, has found a simple way to help people experiencing homelessness in his community. Graham Haskin spent two weeks making and selling bracelets, raising $400 to purchase essential supplies for people in need. With help from his family, he used the money to buy food, bottled water, toilet paper and cleaning supplies for Lowndes Associated Ministries to People Inc. (LAMP), a local organisation that supports people experiencing homelessness. The initiative began with an idea Graham shared with his parents, who helped him turn it into action. His effort has drawn attention for its practical approach to helping others, showing how a child's initiative can support an organisation working to meet the everyday needs of vulnerable people.According to local television station WALB, Graham approached his parents with the idea of making and selling bracelets to raise money for people experiencing homelessness. His father, Justin Haskin, said the initiative came from Graham himself, while the family helped him put the plan into practice.Graham explained that he wanted to be more like Jesus, describing the motivation behind his decision to help others.His parents supported the idea, allowing him to turn a craft he already knew into a fundraising effort.Graham made and sold bracelets over two weeks, raising $400 through the sales. Rather than relying on a conventional donation drive, he chose to make something himself and sell it to raise money for a cause he cared about.The money raised through the bracelet sales went towards food, bottled water, toilet paper and cleaning supplies. With help from his family, Graham delivered the items to Lowndes Associated Ministries to People Inc., commonly known as LAMP.The organisation supports people experiencing homelessness in the Valdosta area. The supplies Graham purchased address everyday needs associated with food, hydration, hygiene and maintaining facilities, providing practical assistance to an organisation working with people who may struggle to access basic necessities.Graham's father, Justin Haskin, told WALB that the idea originated with his son. His mother, Ansley Haskins, also praised the initiative and expressed hope that Graham's actions would encourage other children to find ways to help their communities.Their response highlighted the role of family support in helping children turn an idea into a tangible contribution. While Graham came up with the plan, his parents helped him carry it out, from raising the money to arranging the delivery of supplies.Lowndes Associated Ministries to People Inc. is a nonprofit organisation based in Valdosta, Georgia. It provides services for people experiencing homelessness and others facing hardship in the surrounding region.Through its New Horizons Shelter and Day Center, LAMP offers support that includes emergency shelter for individuals and families. Its work focuses on helping people access essential services and navigate difficult circumstances.LAMP acknowledged Graham's contribution, thanking him for putting his compassion into action. His donation added supplies to the resources available to the organisation as it continues its work in the community.Graham hopes to make and sell more bracelets, while his family hopes his initiative will inspire other children to contribute to their own communities.His first effort raised $400 in two weeks, providing a starting point for any future fundraising he chooses to undertake. The initiative shows how a simple activity can become a means of supporting a local cause when combined with a clear goal and family encouragement.
Article Summary: Graham Haskin made and sold bracelets over two weeks, raising $400. The money went towards food, bottled water, toilet paper and cleaning supplies. The supplies were delivered to Lowndes Associated Ministries to People Inc. (LAMP) The organisation supports people experiencing homelessness in the Valdosta area.

Article Title: Marcelle Flowers, 62, feared AI would take jobs until two young founders solved a $5,000-a-month problem at her plumbing business and made her COO of a startup that raised $52 million
Article Text:
PC: LinkedIn

From BITS Pilani to Broccoli AI: How Jain and Ketkar found a new startup opportunity

How a $5,000 monthly answering service bill helped shape Broccoli AI

Marcelle Flowers helped shape Broccoli AI’s product and public identity

Marcelle Flowers' journey from a single mother to a successful plumbing business leader

What Broccoli AI does for contractors

A $52 million funding round and rapid expansion

At 62, Marcelle Flowers had spent decades building her career in the plumbing industry when two young entrepreneurs arrived at her Sacramento business with an idea for using artificial intelligence. Initially sceptical of the technology, Flowers agreed to test their automated appointment reminder system after recognising a problem it could solve. The meeting soon developed into a working partnership that helped shape Broccoli AI, a startup founded by engineers Jain and Ketkar. Flowers became the company's first chief operating officer, bringing practical industry experience to a business that has since raised $52 million in venture funding and expanded to more than 1,500 customers, as reported by Fortune.Jain and Ketkar had already spent several years trying to establish themselves as entrepreneurs before they began visiting plumbing, heating and electrical contractors in Northern California. According to Fortune reports, the pair met at BITS Pilani in India in 2016 and started working on businesses together the following year. Their earlier ventures included a delivery service for university campuses and an interview preparation programme.After joining Y Combinator, they developed an application programming interface for electric vehicles and moved to London to pursue the idea. They secured eight customers over two years, but the business struggled to grow despite receiving seed funding. The founders moved to San Francisco in January 2024, looking for a different direction.That spring, they began visiting contractors in person, travelling through the Bay Area and into Stockton, Lodi, Modesto and Sacramento. They eventually called on roughly 140 businesses. The founders wanted to understand how smaller trade businesses operated, rather than designing a product from the perspective of a large corporation. They were also looking for an experienced operator who could help them turn what they heard into something useful.Flowers was initially sceptical when her employees told her that two young men were waiting at the counter. She assumed they might be selling fundraising chocolates and was prepared to give them only a few minutes of her time.At 62, she had little enthusiasm for the idea of introducing AI into a business built around human relationships. The founders, meanwhile, had arrived with a simple automated telephone call designed to remind customers about upcoming appointments.The demonstration caught her attention because it addressed a problem she already had. The employee responsible for making those reminder calls had left Armstrong Plumbing, and Flowers had not found a replacement.She agreed to try the product. Within two days, Jain and Ketkar had adapted it using the scripts she supplied. The trial soon moved beyond appointment reminders, however, when Flowers explained that her answering service was a much bigger expense.Reportedly, she was paying about $5,000 a month for the service, which entered bookings into her company's scheduling software only around a third of the time, according to her account. She wanted to know whether the founders could develop a system that handled incoming calls as well. They returned with a working version in about 10 days.For roughly three months, the founders worked from Flowers' Sacramento premises instead of spending all their time at their San Francisco office. She walked them through the daily demands of a contracting business, explaining the language, processes and customer expectations they had not encountered in their engineering careers.Word of mouth took Broccoli AI from its first customer to 10, allowing the founders to reduce their reliance on cold calls. Flowers became an adviser before taking on the role of chief operating officer.She also helped shape the company's public identity, working on its logo, colour scheme and first trade-show booth. Her contribution extended beyond business advice: she had become involved in the company's development at a point when the founders were still deciding what the product should do. Flowers later moved into an apartment in San Francisco to work with the startup.Flowers grew up in Anaheim, California, in a family closely connected to construction. Her father was a commercial plumber whose projects included restaurants, hotels and schools. She became pregnant at 19 and raised her son as a single mother. She has described the years from her mid-teens to her mid-twenties as a period when she made decisions she later regretted. Finding her faith at 26 marked a change in direction, she told Fortune.She joined her father's company in 1995. In 2011, she established its residential service-and-repair operation, which she said grew from approximately $1 million in annual business to $8 million over seven years without outside investment, as reported by Fortune.The business suffered during the COVID-19 period. Flowers said she experienced long COVID for about nine months, while the company's performance deteriorated. She had also previously battled cancer twice, describing both diagnoses as terminal.“I literally said, you have five minutes,” recalled Flowers, now 62 years old. It was June 2024, and a deal to sell her business, Armstrong Plumbing, had fallen through months earlier. She was also “really opposed to AI.”She feared it would take her people and “take all the jobs.”Broccoli AI develops voice-based agents for businesses that provide plumbing, heating, ventilation, air conditioning and electrical services. The software can answer incoming calls, schedule jobs through existing systems, contact customers about outstanding estimates and manage service-membership renewals.These tasks may appear routine, but they can create substantial pressure for small companies. Calls continue to arrive after office staff have left for the day, technicians need to follow up on estimates, and owners must keep track of appointments while managing the work itself.The company says its technology can perform work equivalent to roughly 30% of a typical contractor's office staff. More than 1,500 businesses were using the product at the time of Fortune's report, including Ace Hardware Home Services, Mr. Electric and Any Hour Group.Broccoli AI's growth has attracted significant investor backing. The company raised $22 million in a Series A round and a further $30 million in Series B funding nine months later, bringing the two rounds to $52 million. Khosla Ventures led both, with Y Combinator and Operator Partners also participating.The Series A funding had not previously been announced. The company had earlier secured $1.5 million in seed funding after participating in Y Combinator. According to a person familiar with the matter cited by Fortune, the latest funding placed Broccoli's post-money valuation at $300 million. The company declined to comment on that valuation.Jain said revenue had tripled since the Series A round. The workforce had also expanded considerably, growing from 15 employees a year earlier to more than 150.
Article Summary: Marcelle Flowers helped shape Broccoli AI’s product and public identity. She agreed to test an automated appointment reminder system after recognising a problem it could solve. Flowers became the company's first chief operating officer, bringing practical industry experience to a business that has since raised $52 million.

Article Title: Flávio Bolsonaro declares himself Brazil’s ‘true president’; Trump reacts
Article Text:
File photo: Brazilian senator Flávio Bolsonaro

Poll Vote & Share your view Is Flávio Bolsonaro's comparison to historical leaders like Charles de Gaulle justified? Yes, he is a symbol of resistance No, it's an exaggeration 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Brazilian senator Flávio Bolsonaro has declared himself the country’s “true president-elect”, alleged electoral fraud in President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election and vowed to lead Brazil’s opposition from the United States, where he has arrived with his family after leaving the country.In a lengthy statement addressed to Brazilians and the international community on Wednesday, Flávio rejected the description of his departure as a flight from Brazil, saying he had left to escape what he described as political persecution and an increasingly authoritarian political system. He also thanked US president Donald Trump and Argentine president Javier Milei for their support, portraying the United States as a place where his family could find the legal security he claimed was no longer available at home.“I want to make this clear: I did not flee Brazil; I left for Brazil’s sake” – he wrote, arguing that remaining in the country would have prevented him from exercising political leadership.Flávio alleged that the October 25 presidential election was marred by fraud, claiming that Lula gained more than 10 million votes between the first and second rounds in what he called a “mathematical impossibility”. He also challenged a decision to extend voting hours in some locations, accused judicial authorities of acting beyond their jurisdiction and argued that alleged campaign violations justified annulling the Lula-Alckmin ticket.He claimed that those responsible for what he described as a stolen election belonged to a criminal organisation that had established a ‘tyranny’ in Brazil.Flávio’s claims came as Trump described Brazil’s presidential election as “very strange”, though the US president stopped short of endorsing the senator’s claim that he was the legitimate winner.Asked about Flávio’s assertion that he was the “true president-elect”, Trump said: “I'm not going to make a comment about that...I won't get involved. It was a very strange election, that's for sure.”Flávio’s statement, however, did not provide evidence establishing that electoral fraud had occurred. Brazil’s Liberal Party (PL), which backed Flávio’s candidacy, had earlier recognised the official election result while calling for the issues raised by the campaign to be addressed through political and democratic debate.Meanwhile, US president Donald Trump has described Brazil’s presidential election as 'very strange'. Asked about Flávio’s claim of being the “true president-elect”, Trump said, “I'm not going to make a comment about that...I won't get involved. It was a very strange election, that's for sure.”He also accused the Supreme Federal Court of orchestrating a campaign of political persecution against him and his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro. He claimed that judicial action against him could progress from passport seizure to electronic monitoring, censorship, house arrest and eventual political conviction. He insisted that no arrest warrant had been issued against him and denied committing any crime.The senator said he had brought his family to the US to protect them and would continue his political activities from abroad. Drawing comparisons with figures including French wartime leader Charles de Gaulle and Venezuelan opposition leaders, he portrayed his departure as a continuation of a struggle for democracy rather than an abandonment of Brazilian politics.Addressing lawmakers and governors allied with him, Flávio said he would lead the opposition from the US, promising to speak on behalf of supporters who, he claimed, could not freely express themselves in Brazil. He named senator Rogério Marinho as his candidate for the presidency of the Senate and said he would soon outline a strategy to mobilise the opposition through what he described as peaceful and legitimate means.The statement marks a further escalation in Flávio’s challenge to Lula’s victory. He had previously said he would seek the annulment of the election, while the PL subsequently acknowledged the result proclaimed by Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court.
Article Summary: Brazilian senator Flávio Bolsonaro has declared himself the country’s ‘true president-elect’ He alleged electoral fraud in President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's re-election. He has vowed to lead Brazil's opposition from the United States. US president Donald Trump has described the election as ‘very strange’

Article Title: 'The whole tide turned': Trump takes credit for Netanyahu's showing in Israel elections
Article Text:
Trump claims endorsement turned the tide for Netanyahu

US president Donald Trump has claimed that his endorsement helped Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu turn the tide in Israel’s 26th Knesset election, contributing to the incumbent’s better-than-expected performance. Partial results showed Netanyahu’s bloc leading the race but falling short of the majority needed to form a government.With 57.3% of ballot boxes counted as of 7:58 am, partial results released by the Central Elections Committee showed the pro-Netanyahu bloc securing 55 seats, against 49 for the anti-Netanyahu bloc. Arab parties were projected to win 16 seats.Meanwhile, Reservists, with 2.6% of the vote, People of Israel, with 1.7%, and Charedi Public, with 0.2%, remained below the 3.25% electoral threshold required to enter the Knesset. Votes cast in double envelopes, including those of soldiers, are counted later.On Wednesday, Trump took to Truth Social, where he shared comments by Irving C Schwartz, “When President Trump endorsed Bibi Netanyahu, the whole tide turned, and now, rather than a decisive defeat for a Great Prime Minister, it looks like a big come-from-behind stalemate, or even a WIN for Netanyahu."It all took place AFTER the Endorsement by President Trump, who only wants what is good for the Middle East, Israel, and the United States of America!”Additionally, The Jerusalem Post reported that, while speaking to reporters on the tarmac near Air Force One after attending a rally in Texas, Trump said the Israeli leader had exceeded expectations.“I heard the poll numbers were wrong..., the exit polls; I heard he [Netanyahu] did very well. It was pretty close, but very well. When the endorsement went out, it helped him a lot,” Trump said.He added, “It's a little bit early, but I'm hearing in Israel, top people say, 'Wow! He did a lot better than people thought.' It's looking like maybe a stalemate or a win.”The remarks came after Netanyahu publicly highlighted Trump’s support ahead of the election. In a televised appearance late on Sunday night, the Israeli prime minister praised the US president’s backing.“US President Donald Trump has come with a friendship that has never existed before between an Israeli prime minister and an American president. And it is doubtful we will ever have such a friendly president again,” Netanyahu said.“He has another two years, and he says he is calling on you to vote for me.”Trump had urged Israelis to back Netanyahu in a social media post on Sunday, writing: “Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister, we have to finish the job that we started!”Netanyahu also suggested that the two countries could take further action against Iran, saying Trump was willing to act “that would finally, finally, remove the Iranian threat”. He added that he had instructed Israel’s intelligence agency, Mossad, and the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) to pursue regime change in Iran.Meanwhile, the exit polls suggested that Netanyahu’s bloc and Eisenkot’s each won about 51 seats, and Arab parties won about 18. Netanyahu called for a right-wing government, claiming his bloc had a “significant, decisive majority” among Jewish voters and those supporting a Jewish state.
Article Summary: US president Donald Trump has claimed that his endorsement helped Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu turn the tide in Israel's 26th Knesset election. Partial results showed Netanyahu’s bloc leading the race but falling short of the majority needed to form a government. With 57.3% of ballot boxes counted, partial results showed the pro-Netanyahu bloc securing 55 seats, against 49 for the anti-Net Netanyahu bloc.

Article Title: ​Richard Sackler and his wife tried to stop the sale of their Connecticut mansion, pledged toward Purdue Pharma's $7.4 billion opioid settlement; on October 28, a bankruptcy judge rejected both reques
Article Text:
Sackler’s leadership at Purdue Pharma remains closely linked to OxyContin’s controversial marketing and the company’s legal battles.

A home at the centre of a larger reckoning

The court says the sale must continue

Selling a house that is still occupied

The Sackler fortune under scrutiny

What happens to the Greenwich Mansion

A grand Greenwich residence is rarely the kind of place one expects to find at the centre of a bankruptcy dispute. Yet Richard Sackler and Lin Gao’s Connecticut mansion has become one of the most closely watched properties in the continuing financial fallout from Purdue Pharma and the US opioid crisis. The home at 60 Field Point Circle is now tied to the Sackler family’s obligations under a $7.4 billion settlement involving opioid claimants. On October 28, US Bankruptcy Judge Sean Lane rejected efforts by Sackler and Gao to prevent the property from being sold, keeping the mansion within the pool of assets being used to fund the settlement. Reuters reports that Lane had previously determined the Greenwich residence was among the assets pledged by Sackler family members as collateral for their commitments under the agreement.The property dispute is only one part of a much broader reckoning involving the family that once owned Purdue Pharma. The pharmaceutical company became one of the most recognisable names in the opioid crisis through its aggressive marketing of OxyContin, a prescription painkiller that became central to the national addiction epidemic.Purdue's bankruptcy followed tens of thousands of lawsuits brought by states, municipalities and other parties over the company's role in the crisis.The resulting settlement requires the Sackler family to provide much of the funding, with a substantial portion directed towards state and local governments. According to Reuters, the Greenwich mansion was transferred from one Sackler family trust to another as part of efforts to free up money for a $62 million settlement payment.Sackler and Gao sought to challenge the earlier ruling concerning the property and asked the court to temporarily stop any sale. Both requests were rejected by Lane during Wednesday's hearing. The judge's decision means the property remains subject to the process of converting pledged assets into funds for the settlement. Reuters reports that Lane viewed the couple's attempts to interfere with the sale as inconsistent with the obligations they had undertaken as part of the settlement arrangements.The ruling does not require Sackler and Gao to immediately leave the residence. However, the court left open the possibility of further action if the dispute continues, including sanctions or measures affecting their occupancy.The practical side of selling the mansion presents another complication. Gao and her children continue to live at the property, while the residence also contains artwork that forms part of the assets being considered for sale. Reuters reports that the trust overseeing the sale has indicated that the family's continued presence in the home has made the process more difficult. Determining how the residence and its contents can be prepared for sale adds another layer to an already complicated bankruptcy proceeding. Sackler and Gao's lawyers have said they plan to appeal the earlier decision that allowed the property sale to proceed.The dispute also brings renewed attention to Richard Sackler's role at Purdue Pharma. Now 81, he served as the company's president and chairman during its aggressive promotion of OxyContin. Purdue Pharma pleaded guilty twice to deceptive marketing of the drug. Members of the Sackler family, however, were not personally charged with misconduct in connection with those cases.The family's financial settlement has nevertheless placed its assets under sustained scrutiny, turning properties and other holdings associated with the Sackler fortune into potential sources of compensation.For now, the Field Point Circle property remains occupied, but its status has changed dramatically. Rather than simply being a private family residence, it has become part of a court-supervised effort to fulfil financial commitments arising from Purdue Pharma's bankruptcy. Reuters notes that Sackler also owns four other homes, including a primary residence in Florida. The Connecticut mansion, meanwhile, remains caught between private ownership, family occupancy and the demands of a settlement designed to address the enormous human and financial consequences of the opioid crisis.Its eventual sale could therefore represent more than a real-estate transaction. It would mark another step in converting the wealth accumulated during Purdue Pharma's rise into funds connected to the aftermath of America's opioid epidemic.​Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and Realtor
Article Summary: Richard Sackler and Lin Gao's Connecticut mansion has become one of the most closely watched properties in the continuing financial fallout from Purdue Pharma and the US opioid crisis. The home at 60 Field Point Circle is now tied to the Sackler family’s obligations under a $7.4 billion settlement involving opioid claimants. On October 28, US Bankruptcy Judge Sean Lane rejected the couple's attempts to prevent the property from being sold.

Article Title: A Minnesota lake boundary battle dating to 2017 takes a new turn as an appeals court backs a trust's access to Prairie Lake and upholds a ruling that wiped out neighbours' earlier $148,500 trespass aw
Article Text:
Ulvestad and Hammonds will not receive the $148,500 they had earlier been awarded (Representational AI photo)

How Ulvestad and Hammonds initially won

How an old map changed the outcome

Neighbours challenged the decision again

A dispute between neighbours over access to a lake in Minnesota has taken another turn after nearly nine years in court. On Monday, the Minnesota Court of Appeals ruled in favour of the Blackwood Trust, confirming that its property has direct access to Prairie Lake in St. Louis County. The decision is a setback for neighbours Vicky Jo Ulvestad and Lawrence Craig Hammonds, who had earlier won $148,500 after accusing the trust of entering their land without permission. That award has now been cancelled.According to the court judgment , the disagreement began over where one property ends and the other begin. Ulvestad and Hammonds own a piece of land known as Lot 3, while the Blackwood Trust owns the neighbouring Lots 4 and 5. Both sides disagreed over whether Lot 4 reached the lake or whether a portion of Lot 3 stood in its way.What made the matter more confusing was that two surveys of the land gave different answers. A survey carried out in 1997 showed that Lot 4 did not reach Prairie Lake. However, when the same surveyor examined the properties again in 2010, he reached a different conclusion. The newer survey showed that Lot 4 did have access to the lake.After the 2010 survey, the trust built a cabin on its property. Over the next few years, trees were removed, and a path was created through an area that the neighbours believed belonged to them. The disagreement eventually became a legal battle in 2017. The trust initially asked the court for permission to cross Lot 3 to reach the lake. Ulvestad and Hammonds, meanwhile, accused the trust of trespassing and wanted it stopped from entering their land or removing more trees.At first, the court sided with Ulvestad and Hammonds. It accepted their understanding of where the property boundary lay and decided that Lot 4 did not have direct access to Prairie Lake.The neighbours also won their claim that the trust had entered their property without permission. A jury awarded them $49,400, and the court later increased the amount to $148,500.But the dispute did not end there. The trust challenged the decision, maintaining that its land extended all the way to the lake.In December 2024, the Minnesota Court of Appeals found that an important piece of evidence had not been properly considered. It was an old government map from 1870 showing how the land around Prairie Lake had originally been divided.The appeals court asked the lower court to examine this map before deciding the boundary again. This gave the trust another opportunity to establish that its property reached the water.The 1870 map became important because it showed the original layout of the properties surrounding Prairie Lake.It also contained lines showing the lake's shoreline at the time. These are known as meander lines, which show where the water was when the land was first surveyed.However, the shoreline of a lake can change over time. This means the line drawn on an old map does not always mark the exact boundary of a property today. As explained in the court proceedings, landowners whose properties reach a lake can also own the land between the old survey line and the water's edge.To understand where the properties should meet the lake, a surveyor working for the trust studied the historic map and prepared a fresh survey in April 2025.He used a method called the long-lake method, which takes the shape of a lake into account when deciding how the boundaries of neighbouring properties should be drawn. The new survey supported the trust's claim that Lot 4 reached Prairie Lake without crossing Lot 3.After considering the evidence, the lower court accepted the new boundary. It ruled that the trust's property had its own access to the lake. As a result, the neighbours' trespass claims were dismissed, and the earlier $148,500 award was cancelled.Ulvestad and Hammonds disagreed with the new ruling and returned to the appeals court. They argued that the boundary should have been decided using the original 1870 map rather than relying on the survey prepared in 2025. They believed the southern boundary of their property continued in a straight line towards the lake.They also raised concerns about the surveyor whose findings had helped the trust. During the earlier proceedings, the lower court had initially restricted what evidence could be presented. It later allowed additional testimony from the surveyor.The neighbours said this change had left them without a fair opportunity to challenge his findings. They raised another objection as well. An earlier survey supporting their position had been prepared by the former owner of the same surveying company. They questioned how surveys from the same company could reach different conclusions.However, the appeals court did not accept these arguments. The judges found that the neighbours had been given opportunities to present evidence against the surveyor's findings but had not shown how that evidence might have changed the result.The court also found no sufficient reason to prevent the surveyor from giving evidence simply because an earlier survey from the same company had reached a different conclusion.
Article Summary: Neighbours Vicky Jo Ulvestad and Lawrence Craig Hammonds had earlier won $148,500 after accusing the Blackwood Trust of entering their land without permission. That award has now been cancelled. The disagreement began over where one property ends and the other begin. Both sides disagreed over whether Lot 4 reached the lake.

Article Title: In 2014, demolition work next door damaged a Miami woman's home, but her insurer said the policy excluded the loss; 12 years later, a Florida appeals court upheld her victory over the insurer
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Demolition vibrations damaged the home

Insurer cited earth movement and settlement exclusions

Appeals court explains why the exclusions did not apply automatically

Court upholds $240,000 award and prejudgment interest

What happens when construction work on a neighbouring property damages a home, but the homeowner's insurance company refuses to pay for repairs? For Sandra Moise of Miami, Florida, the dispute centred on whether vibrations from demolition work could be excluded under policy provisions covering earth movement and settlement. The damage occurred in March 2014, and the insurer denied her claim that June, setting off a legal battle that continued for years.On October 28, 2026, Florida's Third District Court of Appeal upheld the judgment in Moise's favour against Homeowners Choice Property & Casualty Insurance Company. In its opinion available on Justia, the court concluded that the insurer had not established grounds to overturn the jury's decision. The ruling affirmed a $240,000 damages award, along with prejudgment interest, and addressed the distinction between damage caused by vibrations and damage resulting from actual earth movement.According to the court's opinion, Moise's home was insured under a policy that took effect on May 8, 2013. On March 1, 2014, demolition activity at a neighbouring property allegedly caused vibrations that damaged the house's floors, walls and ceiling.Moise said she was inside the property during the demolition and felt the shaking. She also noticed picture frames moving and later discovered damage to the house. Her initial complaint, filed on August 27, 2014, alleged that the insurer had failed to cover the loss.Homeowners Choice arranged an inspection by Bracken Engineering, which examined the property on May 6, 2014. The insurer's field adjuster inspected it later that month. The company subsequently denied the claim on June 6, 2014, concluding that the damage resulted from material shrinkage or settlement and fell within the policy's exclusions.The insurance policy covered direct physical losses occurring during the policy period, subject to its exclusions. These included damage caused by earthquakes, landslides, sinking or shifting earth, soil expansion or contraction, and the settling or cracking of foundations. The company argued that the damage to Moise's home fell within these provisions. It maintained that the cracks and other problems were attributable to settlement or pre-existing conditions rather than vibrations alone.Moise's expert, Alfredo Brizuela, offered a different explanation. His report stated that the impact of heavy construction equipment at the adjacent property generated vibrations that travelled through the limestone subsoil and affected the home's foundation structure. In an affidavit, Brizuela clarified that the damage resulted from vibrations, rather than actual displacement or movement of the earth. This distinction became central to the dispute because the court distinguished damage caused by vibrations without actual earth movement from damage resulting from earth movement or settlement covered by the policy's exclusions.The trial court denied the insurer's request for summary judgment on the exclusion issue in December 2019. It subsequently restricted certain arguments about whether vibration itself constituted an excluded cause of loss. The case went to a jury trial in November 2022, and the jury found that the damage was not excluded under the policy. Final judgment was entered on May 1, 2024.Homeowners Choice challenged the outcome, arguing that the trial court had wrongly interpreted the policy and restricted evidence relevant to its defence. The Third District Court of Appeal rejected the insurer's arguments. The appellate court considered earlier decisions involving similar insurance provisions. It distinguished cases in which damage resulted from actual earth movement from those in which vibrations or shock waves caused damage without accompanying movement of the earth.The judges noted that the parties had presented conflicting expert evidence. While the insurer's expert attributed the damage to settlement or other conditions, Moise's expert maintained that vibrations alone had caused it. That conflict did not justify overturning the jury's verdict. The court also found no demonstrated prejudice from the trial court's evidentiary rulings. The insurer had been able to present its position that settlement, rather than vibration, caused the damage. Its expert testified at trial that, although vibrations had occurred, they had not caused the damage. The appeals court therefore found no basis to reverse the judgment on these grounds.The insurer also challenged the monetary award, arguing that the operative complaint was framed as a declaratory judgment action and that the trial court had improperly awarded damages. The appellate court disagreed. It noted that Moise's complaint had also sought monetary damages attributable to the loss if the damage was covered. Florida law permits further relief based on a declaratory judgment when necessary or appropriate.The jury had determined damages of $240,000, and the trial court had added prejudgment interest. The appeals court affirmed this part of the judgment as well, upholding the orders under review in all respects. The ruling does not mean that every property damage claim involving construction vibrations must be covered by insurance. Instead, it highlights the importance of establishing the actual cause of damage and examining the precise wording of policy exclusions. In Moise's case, the court upheld the jury's determination that the damage was not excluded under the policy, affirming the judgment in her favour.
Article Summary: Sandra Moise's home was insured under a policy that took effect on May 8, 2013. On March 1, 2014, demolition activity at a neighbouring property allegedly caused vibrations that damaged the house's floors, walls and ceiling. Moise said she was inside the property during the demolition and felt the shaking. She also noticed picture frames moving and later discovered damage to the house. Her initial complaint alleged that the insurer had failed to cover the loss.

Article Title: ‘$250 protesters’: Trump reacts as hecklers disrupt his rally raising slogans on Epstein - watch
Article Text:
Trump is interrupted by 2 hecklers in a row just minutes into his Ohio rally

US President Donald Trump was interrupted by two hecklers in quick succession during a rally in Ohio, with one shouting that Trump had travelled on Jeffrey Epstein 's plane, prompting the president to accuse the disruptors of being paid protesters.Responding to the heckler, Trump claimed that the man had been paid $250 to disrupt the event and described him as someone following the “radical left playbook”. Trump also brought up his past association with Epstein, the late convicted sex offender, claiming that he had thrown him out of a club around 20 years ago.Trump said: "You know, there's a guy, not a young guy, they gave him $250. Paid Protesters paid. Such. Such losers. Boy, you look at that guy. So that guy, he's right out of the radical left playbook. He's right out of the radical. This guy. This guy was very nondescript. But I will say this. You know, he mentioned Epstein. So I threw Jeffrey Epstein out of a club like 20 years ago because I thought he was a whack job."The interruptions came as Trump addressed the crowd at the Ohio rally. The hecklers' remarks disrupted his speech, prompting him to respond directly to the protesters.Trump has repeatedly alleged, without providing evidence, that people who interrupt his rallies are paid agitators. During the exchange, he also referred to the claim that protesters receive $250 for disrupting his events.In a separate incident reported by the Daily Mail, a heckler interrupted Trump during a rally in Mississippi on Monday, telling him: "Shove that ballroom up your fat a--," in an apparent reference to the planned construction of a new ballroom at the White House.Trump responded by telling the heckler to leave, saying: "Oh, go home," and "Go home, go home."He subsequently claimed that the protesters were being paid, saying: "He gets paid, you know they're paid protesters, they get paid $250 by, they think it's Soros."Trump was referring to billionaire George Soros, a major donor to Democratic and liberal causes. However, the president has not publicly provided evidence to substantiate his claims that the hecklers were paid to disrupt his rallies.
Article Summary: Trump interrupted by two hecklers in quick succession during Ohio rally. One heckler shouted that Trump had travelled on Jeffrey Epstein's plane. Trump claimed that the man had been paid $250 to disrupt the event and described him as someone following the ‘radical left playbook’

Article Title: A California couple bought a home with a 20-by-20-foot garden, then a neighbour claimed the land; a 1955 deal involving $250 and babysitting helped secure their exclusive gardening rights in an Octobe
Article Text:
Rupert Clayton and Miriam Pinchuk bought their Oakland home in 2019, unaware that their neighbours would later claim ownership of its garden. (AI image)

A garage, $250 and a babysitting arrangement

How new neighbours became involved

What the court discovered

Why Canada and Rodriguez lost appeal

A small garden became the centre of a legal battle between two California couples after a property survey revealed that the land belonged to a neighbouring house. Rupert Clayton and Miriam Pinchuk had bought their Oakland home in 2019 believing that the 20-by-20-foot garden was included in the property. But their neighbours, Herbert Canada and Bernadette Rodriguez, claimed the land was legally theirs. The dispute eventually reached the California Court of Appeal, which ruled on Monday that Clayton and Pinchuk could continue using the garden exclusively.According to the California Judicial Branch , the disagreement was unusual because the garden had been separated from the neighbouring property for decades. A retaining wall and fence stood between the two homes, making the disputed area appear to be part of Clayton and Pinchuk's backyard. Thick vegetation also made it difficult to access the garden from the other property.When the couple bought their house, the garden was already well maintained. They considered it an important part of their new home and began using it regularly.However, the confusion had begun long before either couple moved into the neighbourhood. The answer to why the garden was enclosed within one property but legally belonged to another lay in an agreement made in 1955.In the 1950s, the two properties belonged to the Reom and Kroeger families. The Kroegers wanted to replace their garage, but their plans would interfere with an alleyway that the Reoms had the right to use.The families eventually reached an arrangement that allowed the construction to go ahead. The Reoms agreed to surrender their alleyway access rights, while the Kroegers agreed to give them a small section of land.The agreement also involved a payment of $250 and babysitting services provided by Carol Reom for the Kroegers' young child.Following the arrangement, the Kroegers built their new garage and put up a retaining wall and fence. The small piece of land was enclosed within the Reom family's backyard, where it remained for decades.Harry and Carol Reom continued using the area as a garden for more than 50 years. But although the two families had reached an agreement, the necessary property records were never properly completed, according to the findings later examined in court.That missing paperwork became important when the houses changed hands and the new owners began questioning where one property ended and the other began.Canada and Rodriguez purchased the Piedmont property in 2017. Two years later, Clayton and Pinchuk bought the adjoining Oakland house from the Reom family trust.Before the second sale, however, Canada had already been in contact with the Reom family over a separate matter.In 2018, he needed permission to connect to a drainage pipe on their property for renovation work. During those discussions, Larry Reom, the son of Harry and Carol, told him about the old land agreement and provided a document describing it.Larry later testified that Canada had indicated he would have the document officially recorded. The Reom family subsequently allowed the drainage connection without asking for payment.The garden issue came up again in 2020, when Clayton and Pinchuk discussed replacing the boundary fence with their neighbours. Canada showed them a survey indicating that the garden was legally part of his property.This came as a surprise to the couple, who had believed that the garden was included in their purchase.The disagreement continued until December 2021, when Canada contacted the police and reported that Clayton and Pinchuk were trespassing. The couple stopped using the garden while they pursued the matter in court.By the time the case went to trial, the people who had made the original arrangement in 1955 were no longer available to explain what had happened. The court therefore had to rely on surviving documents and testimony from family members.Larry Reom said he had seen a written record of the agreement among his parents' papers, but he could not locate it when the case was heard. Other documents, including old correspondence, supported the account that the families had agreed to exchange the garden area for money, babysitting, and the surrender of alleyway access rights.The court also considered how the land had been used since the 1950s. The Reom family had maintained the garden for decades, while the wall and fence had kept it physically separate from the Kroeger property.After hearing the evidence, the trial court decided that Clayton and Pinchuk should be allowed to continue gardening there, even though it could not establish that ownership of the land had been legally transferred.It granted them an equitable easement, a legal right allowing someone to use another person's land for a particular purpose without owning it.Canada and Rodriguez challenged the trial court's decision, arguing that the couple should not have been given exclusive gardening rights over land that legally belonged to them.The appeal required the judges to consider whether allowing Clayton and Pinchuk to keep using the garden would be fair, given the history of the two properties.One important consideration was how much the couple stood to lose. They had bought their home believing that the garden was included and had spent two years developing it. The area also had fertile soil and was among the flattest parts of their backyard.The court found that Canada and Rodriguez had made little use of the disputed land. Their drainage needs had also been addressed through the separate permission granted by the Reom family.The judges considered the 1955 arrangement particularly important because the previous owners of the neighbouring property had already benefited from it by being able to build their garage. The appellate court ultimately agreed with the trial court's assessment and upheld its decision.
Article Summary: Rupert Clayton and Miriam Pinchuk bought their Oakland home in 2019. They believed that the 20-by-20-foot garden was included in the property. But their neighbours, Herbert Canada and Bernadette Rodriguez, claimed the land was legally theirs. The dispute reached the California Court of Appeal, which ruled on Monday that Clayton and Pinchesuk could continue using the garden exclusively.

Article Title: Trump’s DHS hit by data breach as hackers expose records of 41,000 employees
Article Text:
The officers have faced scrutiny for wearing masks and sunglasses during operations and for failing to clearly identify themselves.

DHS acknowledges potential breach

More than 41,000 employees and contractors of the US department of homeland security (DHS), including thousands of immigration and border enforcement personnel, have had their work details exposed in a major data leak amid growing protests and criticism over President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.The officers have faced scrutiny for wearing masks and sunglasses during operations and for failing to clearly identify themselves.The leaked information includes names, work addresses, phone numbers and job descriptions of personnel working across several agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), a BBC report reveals.The leaked records were published in a searchable online database called “Icepick” on Wednesday. The activist group department of peace said it accessed the information through a single sign-on service used by DHS employees, while cybersecurity researcher Maia Arson Crimew and the nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets helped make the data public.A DHS spokesperson said the department was “aware of a potential breach” and was working to address the situation. The spokesperson added that the agency takes security threats against its employees and officers seriously and would provide further updates when more information became available.According to the leaked data, more than 21,000 personnel listed work for CBP, while nearly 6,600 are associated with ICE. Other records reportedly cover employees of homeland security investigations, the federal protective service and the cybersecurity and infrastructure security agency.The groups behind the disclosure, however, said the database was not intended to be a comprehensive directory of all DHS employees. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets.
Article Summary: More than 41,000 employees and contractors of the US department of homeland security (DHS) have had their work details exposed in a major data leak. Leaked information includes names, work addresses, phone numbers and job descriptions of personnel working across several agencies. The officers have faced scrutiny for wearing masks and sunglasses during operations and for failing to clearly identify themselves.

Article Title: Venezuela's 2016 bond deal put 50.1% of US oil refiner Citgo's parent up as security, now a US appeals court has rejected its bid to void the debt as a separate sale plan earmarks over $2 billion for
Article Text:
A US federal appeals court on Tuesday upheld the validity of bonds issued by Venezuela’s state-owned oil company Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA)

A US federal appeals court on Tuesday upheld the validity of bonds issued by Venezuela’s state-owned oil company Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) that defaulted in 2019, ruling that the transaction did not require prior approval from the country’s National Assembly.The US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed a lower court judgment that found the bonds enforceable under Venezuelan law. The ruling is significant because the bonds are secured by a 50.1% equity interest in CITGO Holding, the parent company of US oil refiner CITGO Petroleum, potentially allowing creditors to pursue the collateral to recover their dues.The decision follows a prolonged legal dispute over whether PDVSA had the constitutional authority to issue the bonds without legislative approval. The company and related entities had sought to have the transaction declared void, arguing that it violated Venezuela’s Constitution.The bonds traded flat on Tuesday at 114.25 cents on the dollar.The case centres on a 2016 bond exchange through which holders of PDVSA’s unsecured notes due in 2017 could exchange them for new, secured notes due in 2020. PDVSA offered the exchange as its financial position deteriorated following a significant fall in crude oil prices between 2014 and 2016.Holders representing about 39.4% of the outstanding principal on the earlier notes accepted the offer. In return, the new bonds were secured by a 50.1% equity interest in CITGO Holding, which PDVSA owned through a chain of subsidiaries.PDVSA’s board approved the exchange in September 2016, along with the relevant approvals from the Venezuelan government as its sole shareholder and the boards of its subsidiaries involved in the transaction.However, Venezuela’s National Assembly, then controlled by opposition parties, challenged the arrangement. It argued that Article 150 of the Venezuelan Constitution required legislative approval for national public interest contracts involving foreign companies.The assembly passed resolutions in 2016 rejecting the use of CITGO shares as collateral and, in October 2019, reiterated that the bond agreement violated the Constitution. PDVSA subsequently failed to make scheduled principal and interest payments on the 2020 notes in October 2019, triggering the dispute.PDVSA, its subsidiary PDVSA Petróleo and holding company PDV Holding argued that the bond exchange and the pledge of CITGO shares were invalid because the National Assembly had not authorised the transaction. They also contended that the assembly’s resolutions should be recognised by US courts under the act-of-state doctrine, which can prevent courts from questioning certain official acts of foreign sovereigns.The US District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled in favour of the creditors in September 2025. It concluded that the transaction was valid under Venezuelan law and that the act-of-state doctrine did not apply.The Second Circuit upheld that judgment. In examining Venezuelan constitutional law, the appeals court relied on interpretations by Venezuela’s Constitutional Chamber indicating that national public interest contracts requiring legislative approval are those entered into by the Republic or competent organs of the National Executive.
